## **The Double-Edged Sword of Generative AI**

The emergence of generative AI represents one of the most transformative technological revolutions in recent history. However, with great power comes significant risks of generative AI that organizations must recognize and address.  
  
These sophisticated systems, capable of creating human-like text, images, code, and more, offer unprecedented opportunities for innovation and efficiency. Nevertheless, the risks continue to mount as adoption accelerates across industries without adequate safeguards.

### **The Rapid Rise of Generative AI**

The past few years have witnessed an explosive growth in [generative AI](https://americanchase.com/generative-ai/) capabilities and adoption. According to a 2024 [Gartner report](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-10-11-gartner-says-more-than-80-percent-of-enterprises-will-have-used-generative-ai-apis-or-deployed-generative-ai-enabled-applications-by-2026), over 80% of enterprises are now experimenting with or implementing generative AI solutions, a dramatic increase from just 30% in 2022.  
  
Furthermore, investment in generative AI technologies surpassed $25 billion in 2023 alone, highlighting the tremendous commercial interest in these tools. However, this rapid acceleration brings with it a corresponding increase in the risks of generative AI deployment across organizations of all sizes.

### **Why Risk Management Is Critical for AI Success**

Managing the risks is not merely a compliance exercise, it’s essential for sustainable business adoption. Research by [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai-in-2023-generative-ais-breakout-year) indicates that organizations with robust AI risk management frameworks are 2.5 times more likely to achieve significant value from their AI investments.  
  
Additionally, the potential costs of mismanaged AI risks can be enormous, with data breaches involving AI systems costing companies an average of $4.45 million per incident in 2023, according to IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report.

### **The Four Major Categories of Generative AI Risk**

To effectively manage the risks of generative AI, it’s essential to understand that these risks fall into four distinct categories: enterprise risks, capability risks, adversarial risks, and marketplace/infrastructure risks. Each category presents unique challenges that require targeted strategies and controls.

## **Enterprise Risks: Protecting Data and Organizational Operations**

Enterprise risks of generative AI encompass threats to an organization’s data security, intellectual property, and operational integrity. These risks demand immediate attention as they can directly impact business continuity and compliance posture.

### **Data Privacy and Confidentiality Concerns**

The risks of generative AI related to data privacy cannot be overstated in today’s regulatory environment. Organizations leveraging these technologies must navigate complex challenges involving data protection and confidentiality.  
  
Unauthorized data exposure represents one of the most significant risks of generative AI deployment. When sensitive information is processed through [AI business strategy](https://americanchase.com/build-ai-program-for-business/) systems, there’s always a possibility that this data might be inadvertently memorized, regurgitated, or leaked in responses to unrelated queries.  
  
For instance, a 2023 study by [Stanford](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/13-biggest-ai-stories-2023) researchers discovered that up to 3% of generative AI outputs contained verbatim snippets from training data, including potentially sensitive information.

### **Intellectual Property Risks**

The intellectual property risks of generative AI present complex challenges for organizations developing, deploying, or using these technologies.  
  
Training data provenance concerns represent another significant dimension of the intellectual property risks of generative AI. Many generative AI systems are trained on vast datasets scraped from the internet, often without explicit permission from content creators. Subsequently, this raises questions about the legitimacy of the resulting AI capabilities and the outputs they produce.  
  
Furthermore, without proper guardrails and review processes, businesses may unknowingly distribute infringing material, creating significant legal exposure.

### **Shadow AI and Unsanctioned Use**

The proliferation of easily accessible generative AI tools has created significant risks associated with unauthorized or unmanaged AI use within organizations.  
  
Employee use of public AI tools with sensitive data represents one of the most pressing risks of generative AI in the enterprise context.  
  
A 2023 survey by [Deloitte](https://www.deloitte.com/ch/en/about/press-room/ai-study-almost-half-of-all-employees-are-worried-about-losing-their-jobs.html) found that 67% of employees have used public generative AI tools for work purposes, with 41% admitting to inputting company data into these systems.  
  
Consequently, sensitive information ranging from customer data to proprietary business strategies may be exposed through these unsanctioned interactions.  
  
Lack of oversight and governance compounds these risks, as many organizations have yet to implement comprehensive policies governing generative AI use.  
  
Furthermore, the ease of access to these tools makes traditional security controls ineffective without specialized monitoring capabilities.

## **Generative AI Capability Risks: When AI Systems Fail**

Beyond enterprise concerns, without clear guidelines, monitoring systems, and enforcement mechanisms, employees may not understand the potential consequences of sharing sensitive data with third-party AI tools.  
  
Thus, the inherent limitations of current generative AI technologies introduce additional risks related to their core functionality and reliability.

### **AI Hallucinations and Misinformation**

The tendency of generative AI systems to produce convincing but fabricated information represents one of the most significant risks of generative AI deployment.  
  
Consequently, when presented with ambiguous prompts or asked to produce information on topics with limited representation in their training data, these systems may generate plausible-sounding but entirely fictional responses, presenting them with the same confidence as factual information.  
  
Detection and prevention strategies for AI hallucinations remain an active area of research and development.  
  
Current approaches include implementing fact-checking mechanisms, maintaining human oversight for critical applications, and designing systems to express appropriate uncertainty when operating beyond their knowledge boundaries.

### **Prompt Injection Attacks**

The vulnerability of risks of generative AI systems to manipulation through carefully crafted inputs represents another significant category of risks.  
  
How attackers manipulate AI through carefully crafted prompts involves exploiting the fundamental architecture of these systems.  
  
By incorporating specific instructions or contextual elements within seemingly innocuous queries, attackers can potentially override system safeguards or extract sensitive information.  
  
Moreover, these attacks are particularly concerning because they target the primary interface through which legitimate users interact with AI systems, making them difficult to prevent without impacting normal functionality.

### **Data Poisoning and Model Tampering**

The integrity of generative AI systems can be compromised through manipulation of their training data or direct interference with their operational parameters.  
  
How attackers can corrupt training data presents a significant risk for organizations developing or fine-tuning AI models from the risks of generative AI.  
  
In data poisoning attacks, adversaries introduce carefully crafted examples into training datasets that cause the model to learn harmful behaviors or biases that only emerge under specific circumstances.  
  
As a result, affected models may appear to function normally in most situations but produce dangerous outputs when triggered by particular inputs or contexts.

### **Accuracy and Reliability Issues**

Even without malicious interference, generative AI systems face inherent challenges related to their accuracy and reliability.  
  
Model limitations and inherent biases stem from the fundamental nature of how these systems are developed and trained. Research has consistently shown that generative AI systems reflect and sometimes amplify biases present in their training data.  
  
Moreover, these biases under the risks of generative AI can manifest in subtle ways that evade detection during standard quality assurance processes.

## **Adversarial AI Risks: Weaponization of AI Technology**

Beyond accidental failures, the risks of generative AI include deliberate exploitation by malicious actors seeking to cause harm or extract value through technological attacks.

### **Advanced Phishing and Social Engineering**

The capabilities of generative AI have dramatically enhanced the sophistication and scale of social engineering attacks.  
  
AI-generated personalized attacks represent a significant evolution in phishing techniques under risks of generative AI.  
  
Unlike traditional approaches that relied on generic templates with obvious red flags, generative AI enables attackers to create highly personalized messages that mimic the writing style, reference specific details, and address individual concerns of targeted victims.

### **AI-Generated Malware and Cyber Attacks**

The scaling of cyberattack capabilities represents perhaps the most significant risk in this category. Traditionally, sophisticated attacks required substantial expertise and manual effort, limiting their prevalence.  
  
In contrast, generative AI enables less skilled attackers to execute advanced techniques and simultaneously target multiple organizations.  
  
Additionally, the automation capabilities reduce the marginal cost of each attack, making mass campaigns economically viable even with lower success rates per target, considering the risks of generative AI.

### **Deep Fakes and Impersonation Fraud**

The ability of generative AI to create convincing simulations of real people introduces unprecedented risks for identity verification and trust.  
  
Voice and video manipulation technologies under risks of generative AI, have advanced dramatically in recent years, with generative AI systems now capable of creating synthetic media that is increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic recordings.  
  
A demonstration by security researchers showed that 83% of participants failed to identify AI-generated video impersonations of colleagues when the content was contextually appropriate.  
  
The financial fraud implications of these technologies are already materializing across multiple sectors. In a notable 2023 case, attackers used AI-generated voice cloning to impersonate a CEO in a call to the company’s finance department, successfully authorizing a fraudulent transfer of $25 million.

## **Marketplace and Infrastructure Risks: The Broader Impact**

Beyond direct security concerns, the risks of generative AI extend to broader ecosystems, regulatory frameworks, and resource requirements.

### **Regulatory Uncertainty and Compliance Challenges**

The rapidly evolving landscape of AI governance creates significant challenges for organizations implementing generative AI solutions.  
  
Current and emerging AI regulations vary substantially across jurisdictions, creating a complex compliance environment for organizations operating globally.  
  
The European Union’s AI Act, China’s comprehensive AI governance framework, and various state-level regulations in the United States each impose different requirements and restrictions.  
  
Furthermore, these regulatory frameworks continue to evolve as lawmakers and regulators develop a deeper understanding of the risks of generative AI.

### **Computing Infrastructure and Energy Concerns**

The resource requirements for developing and deploying generative AI systems introduce additional risks related to cost, availability, and environmental impact.  
  
Computational resource demands for state-of-the-art generative AI continue to increase at an exponential rate.  
  
According to estimates from AI researchers, the computational requirements for training leading models have doubled approximately every 3-4 months since 2021, far outpacing Moore’s Law.  
  
Consequently, organizations developing custom models face significant infrastructure challenges under the risks of generative AI that may limit their ability to compete with larger, better-resourced competitors.

### **Vendor Lock-in and Technology Obsolescence**

The rapidly evolving nature of generative AI creates strategic risks related to technology choices and partnerships.  
  
Integration challenges across platforms complicate efforts to diversify provider relationships or transition between technologies.  
  
Each system has unique risks of generative AI along with capabilities, limitations, and interfaces, making interoperability difficult without significant investment in abstraction layers and standardization.  
  
Furthermore, outputs from different systems may have subtle but important differences that complicate efforts to use them interchangeably.

## **Building an Effective AI Risk Management Framework**

Addressing the multifaceted risks of generative AI requires a comprehensive framework that combines governance, technical controls, and responsible development practices. Effective management of generative AI risks begins with clear governance structures and accountability.

### **Governance and Organizational Structure**

C-suite responsibilities for AI oversight should be clearly defined, with specific executive roles assigned ownership of different aspects of AI governance.  
  
While the specific structure varies by organization, common approaches include assigning primary responsibility to the CIO, CISO, or a dedicated Chief AI Officer, with supporting roles for legal, compliance, privacy, and business leadership.  
  
Furthermore, executive-level engagement ensures that the risks of generative AI management receive appropriate attention and resources.

### **Technical Controls and Safeguards**

Beyond governance structures, effective management of generative AI risks requires implementation of technical controls tailored to these technologies.  
  
Model firewalls and input validation mechanisms provide the first line of defense against many risks of generative AI.  
  
Properly implemented input controls can prevent sensitive data from being processed by AI systems, block prompt injection attacks, and ensure that interactions remain within approved use cases.  
  
Moreover, these controls should be regularly tested and updated to address evolving attack techniques and use patterns.

### **Responsible AI Development Practices**

Long-term management of risks of generative AI requires embedding responsible practices throughout the AI lifecycle.  
  
Ethical AI principles and implementation frameworks provide the foundation for responsible development and use.  
  
Organizations should establish clear principles addressing issues like fairness, transparency, privacy, and human oversight, then translate these principles into specific requirements and practices.  
  
Furthermore, these risks of generative AI should be regularly reviewed and updated to reflect evolving societal expectations and technological capabilities.

## **Role-Specific Strategies for Managing AI Risks**

Different organizational roles approach generative AI risks from unique perspectives, each with specific responsibilities and concerns.

### **Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) Approach**

Security leaders face unique challenges in addressing the novel risks of generative AI introduced by technologies.  
  
AI-specific security frameworks extend traditional security models to address the unique characteristics of generative AI systems.  
  
Effective frameworks typically address four key dimensions: protecting AI systems from attack, preventing AI systems from being used as attack vectors, ensuring data security throughout the AI lifecycle, and maintaining appropriate access controls and authentication mechanisms.  
  
Furthermore, these frameworks should evolve continuously as new risks of generative AI and vulnerabilities emerge.

### **Chief Data Officer and Privacy Officer Perspective**

Data and privacy leaders play crucial roles in ensuring that generative AI deployment respects privacy rights and maintains data integrity.  
  
Privacy-preserving AI techniques provide mechanisms for developing and using generative AI while minimizing the privacy risks of generative AI.  
  
Approaches like differential privacy, federated learning, and homomorphic encryption allow organizations to derive value from data while providing mathematical guarantees about privacy protection.  
  
Additionally, synthetic data generation can enable development and testing with realistic but non-sensitive information, reducing the need to expose real personal data.

### **Legal and Compliance Considerations**

Legal teams face novel risks of generative AI in managing liability and contractual issues related to generative AI deployment.  
  
Contracts with AI vendors should allocate responsibility for issues like data security, intellectual property rights, and compliance with applicable regulations.  
  
Similarly, terms of service for AI-powered products should set appropriate expectations and limitations regarding system performance, permitted uses, and liability for outputs.

## **Future-Proofing Your AI Strategy**

Successful organizations view risk management not as a barrier to innovation but as an enabler of sustainable AI adoption. The rapidly evolving landscape of generative AI requires forward-looking approaches that balance current needs with future flexibility, overshadowingthe  risks of generative AI.

### **Balancing Innovation with Risk Management**

By establishing clear boundaries and controls, risks of generative AI frameworks can accelerate innovation by providing confidence to explore new applications within appropriate guardrails.  
  
Furthermore, effective risk management helps organizations avoid costly mistakes and reputation damage that could undermine long-term AI strategies.  
  
Many organizations are adopting tiered approaches that apply minimal controls to exploratory projects while implementing comprehensive safeguards for systems that process sensitive data or support critical decisions.

### **Staying Current with Evolving AI Capabilities**

Establishing formal technology monitoring processes helps organizations identify relevant innovations before they become widespread.  
  
Effective approaches include dedicated research teams, partnerships with academic institutions, and participation in industry consortia and standards bodies.  
  
Furthermore, monitoring should address not only technical capabilities but also evolving best practices, regulatory developments, and societal expectations of risks of generative AI.

### **Building a Culture of Responsible AI Use**

Successful AI risk management extends beyond formal controls to encompass organizational culture and individual behavior.  
  
Empowering employees to raise concerns about the risks of generative AI creates an essential early warning system for potential issues.  
  
Organizations should establish clear channels for reporting problems, protect those who raise legitimate concerns from retaliation, and ensure that reported issues receive appropriate attention and follow-up.  
  
Furthermore, recognizing and rewarding responsible reporting helps reinforce the importance of speaking up about potential risks.

## **Conclusion: Embracing AI Safely in a Rapidly Changing Landscape**

The risks of generative AI are substantial but manageable with appropriate strategies and controls.  
  
By understanding the diverse challenges across enterprise, capability, adversarial, and marketplace domains, organizations can develop comprehensive approaches that protect against harm while enabling innovation.

### **Key Takeaways for Business Leaders**

Addressing the risks of generative AI requires executive commitment and cross-functional collaboration. Leaders should establish clear governance structures, invest in appropriate controls and safeguards, and foster organizational cultures that balance innovation with responsibility.  
  
Furthermore, ongoing attention to emerging risks and capabilities will be essential as these technologies continue to evolve at a rapid pace.  
  
The costs of ignoring risks of generative AI far outweigh the investments required for effective management. Data breaches, compliance violations, reputational damage, and lost opportunities can all result from inadequate risk management practices.  
  
In contrast, organizations that establish robust frameworks for managing these risks position themselves to realize sustainable value from AI investments while avoiding potential pitfalls.

### **Creating Your AI Risk Management Roadmap**

Developing a comprehensive approach to managing the risks of generative AI typically involves several key stages. Organizations should begin with a current state assessment that identifies existing AI applications, data assets, and control environments.  
  
Next, they should establish governance structures and policies that define roles, responsibilities, and decision rights for AI development and deployment.  
  
Finally, they should implement technical controls, monitoring capabilities, and ongoing review processes to address specific risks and ensure continuous improvement.

### **Resources for Ongoing Education and Support**

As the generative AI landscape continues to evolve rapidly, we at [American Chase](https://americanchase.com/) stay informed about emerging risks, capabilities, and best practices is essential for effective management of the risks of generative AI.  
  
Industry associations, standards bodies, and research organizations provide valuable resources for organizations navigating these challenges.  
  
Investing in internal communities of practice creates sustainable capabilities for addressing the risks of generative AI.  
  
These communities bring together professionals from different functions and business units to share knowledge, develop expertise, and collaborate on solutions to common challenges.  
  
Moreover, they help organizations retain and apply lessons learned across multiple AI initiatives, avoiding repeated mistakes and accelerating progress toward mature risk management practices.

## **FAQs**

### **What are the biggest risks of implementing generative AI in business operations?**

The most significant risks of generative AI in business operations include data privacy breaches, intellectual property complications, AI hallucinations leading to misinformation, and security vulnerabilities like prompt injection attacks.

### **How can organizations protect sensitive data when using generative AI?**

To protect sensitive data when using generative AI, organizations should implement robust data governance frameworks specifically designed for AI systems. This includes clear data classification policies, access controls that limit AI exposure to sensitive information, and monitoring systems that detect potential data leakage.

### **How can businesses defend against prompt injection attacks?**

Defending against prompt injection attacks requires multiple layers of protection. Organizations should implement input validation that screens for potential malicious instructions, establish context boundaries that prevent AI systems from accessing or modifying core instructions, and deploy continuous monitoring to identify unusual interaction patterns.

### **What infrastructure challenges do companies face when scaling generative AI?**

Scaling generative AI introduces significant infrastructure challenges, including escalating computational demands that outpace traditional IT growth patterns. The specialized hardware requirements (particularly high-performance GPUs) create bottlenecks due to global supply constraints and high acquisition costs.

Introduction
------------

In an era of unprecedented technological change, artificial intelligence (AI) continues to reshape global industries. Recent advances in machine learning, generative AI, natural language processing, deep learning and robotics hold transformative potential across sectors, accelerated by increasingly capable (‘frontier’) large language models (LLMs).

Yet, while the integration of AI into business processes remains an exciting prospect, it also presents a rapidly evolving compliance challenge. Organisations must now navigate new regulations and substantial safety concerns, including safeguarding data, ensuring knowledgeable human oversight and adapting risk frameworks for powerful frontier AI models. AI in application can extend across multiple organisational functions and solutions, making it nearly impossible to confine AI risk management and compliance to technology or procurement teams alone. As frontier AI models develop ‘agentic’ capabilities to run distinct processes such as coding and research,[[1]](https://globalinvestigationsreview.com/guide/the-guide-compliance/fourth-edition/article/mastering-ai-compliance-strategies-mitigating-risks-in-rapidly-evolving-landscape#footnote-1) businesses must balance anticipated productivity benefits against the potential for hallucinations, increased complexity and inscrutability.

This chapter explores a high-level overview of the current global AI compliance landscape and provides a summary of the challenges that businesses may encounter and some potential countermeasures. It does not provide a granular view of AI in investigative or enforcement contexts; rather, it aims to outline key considerations for legal practitioners and executives seeking a prudent path through AI compliance.

Challenges of AI compliance
---------------------------

AI compliance presents complex challenges for global organisations, compounded by evolving regulatory frameworks. Below is a high-level overview of as of May 2025, noting that regulatory approaches may change rapidly as regulators address technological developments, especially in generative AI.

### European Union

The European Union continues to lead in comprehensive AI regulation. The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (the EU AI Act), which entered into force on 1 August 2024, is now undergoing a phased implementation, establishing a unified legal framework directly applicable in each EU Member State. The Act maintains its tiered regulatory approach to AI applications based on risk, rather than sector, with initial provisions, such as the ban on AI systems posing an ‘unacceptable risk’ and requirements for AI literacy, having become applicable in February 2025. While the AI Act introduces a comprehensive framework, its most stringent provisions remain targeted. The initial ban on ‘unacceptable risk’ systems, which took effect on 2 February 2025, covers specific practices such as cognitive behavioural manipulation and social scoring.

Significant new obligations are also being developed for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, with rules set to apply from August 2025, and for high-risk AI systems, which are narrowly defined to cover areas like the safety components of certain products and specific AI uses in critical domains such as recruitment or credit assessments, due to come into force in August 2026 (with a later August 2027 date for high-risk AI in safety products).

Determining whether an AI system falls into categories like prohibited, high-risk or GPAI remains critical, as the associated compliance obligations are substantial and penalties for non-compliance can be severe. For instance, providers of high-risk systems face requirements for risk assessments, data quality, record-keeping and human oversight. The establishment of the European AI Office as a central enforcement and guidance body further underscores the importance of diligent compliance.

Beyond the AI Act’s specific requirements, organisations must continue to navigate a complex web of other EU legislation relevant to AI, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), consumer protection laws and intellectual property rights. New and updated directives, such as those concerning product liability and platform work, also intersect with AI governance and must be considered.

Key developments in the past year are as follows.

*   The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, with a staggered implementation schedule. Prohibitions on unacceptable risk AI systems began applying on 2 February 2025, rules for general-purpose AI models take effect on 2 August 2025 and the full Act becomes applicable on 2 August 2026. Organisations have this transitional period to assess their AI systems and implement compliance measures.
*   A central governance body, the European AI Office, was established in May 2024 to oversee implementation and enforcement, particularly for general-purpose AI models. The Office published preliminary guidelines in April 2025, clarifying obligations for GPAI model providers, and is developing a Code of Practice for general-purpose AI models due in May 2025, which will serve as a compliance blueprint.
*   The EU adopted a new Product Liability Directive in October 2024 that explicitly includes software and AI systems as ‘products’ subject to liability rules. This significantly impacts the risk profile for AI developers and users, as it allows consumers to seek compensation for harm caused by defective AI systems in certain circumstances. Member States must implement it by December 2026.

### United Kingdom

The Labour government elected in July 2024 has evolved the UK’s approach to AI regulation, maintaining a pro-innovation stance while introducing more targeted oversight. Unlike the EU’s comprehensive AI Act, the UK is pursuing a balanced strategy focusing on frontier AI models while maintaining regulatory flexibility for the wider AI ecosystem. This approach recognises both the economic potential of AI and emerging concerns about safety and security.

While specific legislation for frontier AI models is under development, the government has established a coordinating framework through the Regulatory Innovation Office to enable more responsive and adaptive regulation across sectors. This approach aims to address the challenge that regulators are often ill-equipped to deal with rapidly evolving technologies that span multiple industries.

The UK continues to build upon the five core principles established by the previous government: safety, security and robustness; transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; and contestability and redress. These principles remain influential despite the shift in regulatory focus. Existing regulators such as the Information Commissioner, the Competition and Markets Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority continue to play critical roles in this governance ecosystem, with their guidance and consultations on AI issues forming an important part of the evolving regulatory landscape.

Key developments in the past year are as follows.

*   In October 2024, the government announced the Regulatory Innovation Office to address, among other areas, AI, with the premise of enabling and supporting greater regulatory collaboration in respect of new technologies.
*   In February 2025, the UK government changed the name of the AI Safety Institute to the AI Security Institute with a renewed focus on national security implications of AI technology. This development signals a stronger emphasis on AI security concerns over broader safety issues.
*   In January 2025, the UK government published its AI Opportunities Action Plan. The plan outlines several key initiatives including the use of regulatory sandboxes for testing AI applications, increased funding for sector regulators to develop AI-specific capabilities and requirements for sector regulators to disclose the ways in which they have promoted AI-related innovation. Nonetheless, the AI Opportunities Action Plan broadly maintains the UK’s commitment to a lighter regulatory approach than the EU’s comprehensive AI Act.

### United States

AI regulation in the United States continues to be largely sector-specific and fragmented at the federal level, with no single comprehensive law governing AI. A significant shift in federal AI policy occurred over the past year, with a move away from the prior government’s focus on risk management and towards establishing a new national policy focused on promoting American AI innovation and reducing regulatory barriers.

Despite this federal policy shift, various agencies continue to address AI. The Federal Trade Commission remains active in tackling AI-related risks concerning consumer protection and unfair competition. The National Institute of Standards and Technology also continues to develop voluntary guidelines and standards to support AI development and deployment.

In contrast, state-level AI regulation has continued to grow. However, the landscape for state-level AI regulation faces potential disruption from a proposed 10-year federal moratorium on the enforcement of state AI laws, advanced by a House Committee in May 2025.

Key developments in the past year:

*   In January 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14179, ‘Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence’, which revoked President Biden’s 2023 Executive Order 14110 on the safe, secure and trustworthy development and use of AI. This new order prioritises sustaining America’s global AI dominance by promoting innovation and removing perceived barriers, marking a shift from the previous administration’s emphasis on risk management.
*   In May 2025, the House Energy & Commerce Committee advanced a provision within a budget reconciliation bill proposing a 10-year moratorium on the enforcement of state AI laws. Proponents argued this was necessary to prevent a fragmented regulatory landscape and allow a ‘learning period’ for a unified federal approach. The moratorium provision was subsequently removed, but its inclusion provides a key example of the ongoing tension between legislating for increasingly ubiquitous AI services at state and federal level.
*   Virginia is poised to enact the High-Risk AI Developer & Deployer Act (HB 2094), which was passed by the Virginia General Assembly in February 2025. This law would establish duties for developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems. Similar to Colorado’s AI Act, this law aims to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination and would require reporting of associated risks, reflecting continued state-level efforts to address AI risks comprehensively.
*   In May 2025, the Department of Commerce’s BIS announced its intention to rescind the Biden-era ‘AI Diffusion Rule’, citing concerns that it could hinder American innovation. Simultaneously, BIS strengthened export controls on semiconductors used for AI and issued guidance on the risks associated with using AI chips developed in China, signalling active use of export controls to manage AI technology dissemination.

### Australia

Australia’s approach to AI regulation, historically rooted in its voluntary AI Ethics Principles, has seen a significant shift towards more formal and potentially mandatory structures since July 2024. There is a clear momentum towards establishing a more structured regulatory environment, particularly for AI use within government and for applications deemed high-risk across the wider economy.

Alongside these initiatives aimed at creating new AI-specific frameworks, Australia is also actively reviewing and amending existing laws, such as those concerning privacy and consumer protection, to better address the challenges posed by AI. Specific legislative action has also been taken to target particular AI-related harms (such as deepfakes), indicating a multi-pronged strategy to govern this evolving technology.

Key developments in the past year:

*   On 5 September 2024, the Department of Industry, Science and Resources released a consultation paper proposing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings, aiming to build public trust and provide regulatory clarity. The paper outlined 10 potential guardrails focusing on accountability, risk management, data governance, testing, human oversight and transparency, and sought input on regulatory models for implementation.
*   The Senate Select Committee on Adopting Artificial Intelligence presented its final report on 26 November 2024, recommending the introduction of new, whole-of-economy, dedicated legislation to regulate high-risk AI uses, potentially an ‘Australian AI Act’. The report also urged a principles-based definition of high-risk AI, including general-purpose AI models, and called for increased support for sovereign AI capability.

### China

China’s strategic and state-driven approach to AI regulation, with ambitions for global leadership by 2030, saw significant expansion since the previous version of this chapter. Building on earlier specific measures for generative AI, algorithmic tools and deepfakes, this period was marked by the finalisation of key binding regulations, primarily addressing the labelling of AI-generated content and broader network data security, including for AI systems, imposing immediate compliance obligations and reinforcing existing frameworks like algorithm filing and data classification.

Alongside these legally binding developments, China also released an AI Safety Governance Framework in September 2024, and draft guidelines for generative AI security incident response (December 2024), indicating a growing emphasis on proactive safety, ethics and incident management. The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) continued active enforcement of AI-related rules, while progress towards a comprehensive national AI Law continued, seeking to balance innovation with effective risk control.

Key developments in the past year:

*   In March 2025, the CAC and other bodies released measures mandating explicit and implicit labelling for AI-generated content, including text, images and video, effective 1 September 2025. These rules apply broadly to service providers and content distributors, including those outside China serving the mainland market, and aim to combat misinformation.
*   The Regulations on Network Data Security Management (NDSM) became effective on 1 January 2025, clarifying and expanding data security obligations with specific relevance to AI data processing, data scraping for training and cross-border data transfers. The NDSM, which have extraterritorial reach, require AI service providers to implement measures against network security risks and assess the legality of data scraping.

### Hong Kong

Over the past year, Hong Kong’s approach to AI regulation continued to mature, favouring the issuance of sector-specific guidelines and ethical frameworks over comprehensive, binding legislation. Government bodies, notably the Digital Policy Office (DPO) and the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD), were active in publishing guidance to promote responsible AI development and deployment, with a strong emphasis on data privacy and ethical considerations. This period also saw significant attention given to the financial services sector, with multiple regulators issuing tailored advice.

In addition to these guidance-led initiatives, Hong Kong progressed with adapting existing legal frameworks, particularly in copyright law to accommodate AI’s use of data. The government also actively fostered AI innovation through new funding schemes and the establishment of research-focused institutions, signalling a dual approach of encouraging technological advancement while addressing emerging risks through primarily non-legislative means.

Key developments in the past year:

*   The DPO released its Ethical AI Framework (Version 1.4) in July 2024 and Generative AI Technical and Application Guideline in April 2025, providing voluntary guidance for responsible AI development and use. Complementing this, the PCPD issued an AI Model Personal Data Protection Framework in June 2024 and a Checklist on Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI by Employees in March 2025, emphasising data protection and ethical considerations in AI deployment.
*   The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau issued a Policy Statement on Responsible Application of AI in the Financial Market in October 2024, followed by circulars from the Securities and Futures Commission in November 2024 on generative AI use and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority on consumer protection (August 2024). Separately, a government discussion paper in February 2025 proposed a text and data mining exception to the Copyright Ordinance to support AI training.

### Japan

Japan’s approach to AI regulation has maintained a strong pro-innovation stance, initially relying on non-binding governance principles and industry self-regulation. There is, however, movement towards a more formalised, albeit still light-touch, framework in the form of a new AI bill. This draft legislation aims to foster AI development through public-private cooperation under a new AI Strategy Headquarters, rather than imposing strict, penalty-backed mandates immediately.

Alongside legislative developments, existing guidelines like the ‘AI Guidelines for Business’ were revised to address emerging risks, particularly from generative AI, and potential amendments to the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) were proposed to facilitate data use for AI training. Sector-specific considerations, notably in finance, also emerged, and Japan continued its active role in international AI governance dialogues, such as the Hiroshima AI Process.

Key developments in the past year:

*   The ‘Bill on the Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technologies’ passed Japan’s House of Councillors in May 2025. It aims to promote AI R&D and protect citizens’ rights through a collaborative framework, establishing an AI Strategy Headquarters. While omitting direct penalties, it allows for public naming of entities infringing rights and includes a resolution to combat deepfake pornography. Concurrently, Version 1.1 of the ‘AI Guidelines for Business’ was released in April 2025, offering updated guidance on risk management, contractual issues and generative AI.
*   In February 2025, Japan’s Personal Data Protection Commission proposed amendments to the APPI to potentially ease consent requirements for using sensitive and third-party personal data for AI model training, provided re-identification risks are low. Additionally, the Financial Services Agency released a discussion paper in March 2025, ‘Preliminary Discussion Points for Promoting the Sound Utilization of AI in the Financial Sector’, signalling potential future sector-specific AI regulations concerning model validation, transparency and oversight, particularly for generative AI.

### Singapore

Singapore continues its pragmatic and innovation-friendly approach to AI governance, emphasising responsible AI adoption through collaboration and sector-specific guidelines rather than introducing new, overarching AI-specific legislation. Building on foundational documents like the Model AI Governance Framework from 2020 and the Model Governance Framework for Generative AI (released in May 2024), this period saw further refinements with updated ethical and governance resources.

New developments focused on enhancing AI safety and security, issuing more detailed guidance for critical sectors such as finance and law, and addressing specific AI-driven risks. For instance, legislation was passed in October 2024 to ban deepfakes of political candidates during election periods. Singapore also maintained a strong commitment to international cooperation on AI governance standards.

Key developments in the past year:

*   In August 2024, the AI Ethics & Governance Body of Knowledge Version 2.0 was released by the Singapore Computer Society and IMDA, expanding guidance to cover Generative AI and more sectors. Further AI safety initiatives were announced in February 2025, including the Global AI Assurance Pilot to test GenAI applications, and the Cybersecurity Agency of Singapore Guidelines on Securing AI Systems in October 2024.
*   The Supreme Court of Singapore issued guidelines on the use of generative AI in court proceedings, effective 1 October 2024, requiring accuracy and accountability. In the financial sector, the Monetary Authority of Singapore released an Information Paper on AI Model Risk Management in April 2025, outlining good practices for managing risks associated with traditional and generative AI models.

### South Korea

South Korea took a landmark step in AI regulation by promulgating the comprehensive Framework Act on Artificial Intelligence Development and Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness (the AI Framework Act) on 21 January 2025. This legislation, the first of its kind in the APAC region and effective from 22 January 2026, signals a shift towards a more formalised, risk-based approach to AI governance, with the aim of balancing the promotion of AI innovation with the need to ensure safety, reliability and public trust, particularly concerning ‘high-impact’ AI systems and generative AI.

The Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) is spearheading the development of subordinate legislation to further define the AI Framework Act’s practical application. In parallel, existing legal frameworks, especially the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA), continue to govern the data protection aspects of AI development and deployment.

Key developments in the past year:

*   South Korea promulgated its landmark AI Framework Act on 21 January 2025, becoming the first APAC nation with comprehensive AI legislation, effective 22 January 2026. The Act introduces a risk-based approach with specific obligations for ‘high-impact’ AI in sectors like healthcare and energy, as well as transparency requirements for generative AI, aiming to balance innovation with safety and trustworthiness.
*   The MSIT is developing subordinate regulations for the AI Framework Act, anticipated in the first half of 2025, which will detail criteria for high-impact AI, specific safety measures and requirements for domestic representatives of foreign AI operators. Concurrently, the Act relies on the PIPA for personal data matters, with the Personal Information Protection Commission actively providing guidelines on PIPA’s application to AI, including for automated decision-making and the use of data in AI training.

### Conclusion

Key jurisdictions are taking divergent approaches to AI regulation, making cross-jurisdiction compliance especially challenging. While the EU leads with specific legislation, many other jurisdictions rely on principles and existing regulatory frameworks. This regulatory divergence requires sustained diligence and companies creating or implementing AI products or solutions will need to be conscious of which jurisdictions those products touch on, and alive to regulatory developments in each of those jurisdictions.

Managing the risks: key concepts
--------------------------------

AI poses several principal risks for global organisations, requiring vigilance, particularly in light of new guidance on frontier models and AI safety.

### Governance

Effective governance mechanisms are essential for managing AI risks. While comprehensive regulation is still developing in most jurisdictions, existing laws (e.g., consumer protection, sectoral regulations) may already apply to AI uses, especially frontier generative AI tools that produce non-deterministic outputs. Organisations should establish AI governance committees to holistically address AI compliance and in particular develop enforceable enterprise-wide policies. We consider below how this might be achieved.

### Ethics and environmental, social and governance issues

The use of AI by companies may also raise significant environmental, social and governance issues and ethical risks. In particular, given the increasing energy consumption associated with AI datacentres, AI’s overall effect on the environment needs to be considered as companies seek to remain compliant with their environmental obligations and commitments – especially in Europe, where ESG reporting requirements continue to expand.

Companies must also continue to be wary of the fact that AI may exacerbate the potential issues already inherent in human decision-making, such as bias, discrimination and inequality. The training data used for AI models can lead to them inheriting human biases contained in that training data so it is important to identify and mitigate this risk, particularly in circumstances where AI may be making decisions that directly affect individuals (e.g., credit scoring or hiring).

More generally, there are difficult societal questions about whether some decisions, especially those implicating fundamental rights, should be delegated to a machine in the first place.

### Data protection and copyright

Data protection remains a front-line concern for generative AI. Statements from various data protection authorities and other regulators increasingly focus on the legality of scraping public data for training large language models. The question of whether such training violates data protection or copyright laws is no longer hypothetical – multiple inquiries and investigations underscore the importance of careful, lawful data sourcing.

There are a number of difficult and unresolved questions about the compatibility of certain AI systems, particularly generative AI systems, with these laws. For example, is it lawful to train these models on public data, particularly if it contains special-category personal data such as political opinions, health information and religious beliefs? Similarly, do these systems breach the accuracy principle in the GDPR given their output can contain ‘hallucinations’, where false or misleading information is presented as fact?

Where personal data is used, standard requirements (e.g., data protection impact assessments, minimising retained personal data, implementing robust controls on automated decision-making) must extend to generative Al.

### Staff compliance

Employee misuse or unintentional disclosure of confidential data to generative AI platforms has become a recurring discussion in compliance circles, particularly in circumstances where a major AI platform provider, OpenAI, was ordered in May 2025 to retain all prompt outputs. Companies will need to consider introducing training on the capabilities and limits of Al models, specifically highlighting the risk of providing sensitive or proprietary data to external AI systems; and policies clarifying that employees remain responsible for verifying LLM outputs rather than deferring to AI-generated conclusions.

Such measures reinforce that, while AI can automate certain tasks, accountability ultimately rests with the employee and the organisation.

We consider further below the need for organisations to invest in training that is directly tailored to the specific corporate environment and tasks in question, and that highlights the risks and limitations of current AI products, as well as policies that make it clear that employees remain responsible and accountable for actions and decisions made using AI systems.

### Operational risks

Frontier AI tools introduce new cybersecurity and operational risks, including ‘prompt injection’ attacks where trusted inputs force AI tools to disclose sensitive data or perform unintended tasks.[[2]](https://globalinvestigationsreview.com/guide/the-guide-compliance/fourth-edition/article/mastering-ai-compliance-strategies-mitigating-risks-in-rapidly-evolving-landscape#footnote-2)Organisations must implement robust security protocols and ensure that third-party AI services meet these standards.

In addition to the data protection risks identified above, the use of AI by organisations can also raise cybersecurity issues. Rapidly advancing technology increases susceptibility to new forms of attack, and given the complexity, opacity and non-deterministic nature of the inner workings of some of the most capable current AI models, it is likely that adversaries will continue to identify new AI attack vectors in the future.

Organisations that rely heavily on AI systems to process large volumes of data, or for algorithmic decision-making, are at risk of operational failures in the event that these systems encounter issues or are subject to attacks.

Addressing and mitigating these risks is beyond the scope of this chapter, but particularly where companies are implementing AI products developed by third parties, it will be important to understand and test what security measures have been implemented in their AI products. That is, again, particularly the case where AI products are processing personal data or making decisions that could directly affect individuals.

Road map to AI compliance
-------------------------

### Introduction

The continued growth of AI adoption underscores the need for forward-looking compliance. Organisations must integrate regulatory updates, AI safety considerations and operational risk management strategies as part of a dynamic compliance programme.

This section provides an overview for legal professionals and business executives on some key aspects of AI governance, including regulatory frameworks, ethical imperatives and risk management strategies that are integral to compliant AI operations. Given the shifting regulatory backdrop noted above and the wide variety of AI applications across different sectors, the guidance presented here is intended to provide a high-level overview of what adherence to legal requirements and responsible AI utilisation might look like rather than being prescriptive. Any compliance framework must also be dynamic, keeping pace with the rapid changes in both regulation and technological advancement.

### Example of an AI compliance framework

#### AI governance

A crucial first step in navigating AI risks is appropriate governance structures, in particular a dedicated AI governance committee, or the expansion of the remit of an existing committee or management body to encompass AI oversight. Such a committee might:

*   define overarching Al principles, including how generative Al may (and may not) be utilised within the organisation;
*   evaluate new Al tools for compliance risks – and assess whether they align with new statutory obligations or regulatory guidance in relevant jurisdictions; and
*   oversee post-deployment usage reviews, especially where advanced LLM output might infringe consumer protection, data protection or antidiscrimination laws.

#### Visibility and control over current use

After establishing a governance framework, companies might concentrate on the existing and proposed AI systems that are being integrated within an organisation. Organisations should assess where AI is already in use, including generative AI platforms introduced informally by employees. Practical steps include:

*   an Al deployment inventory: track which business units rely on generative Al outputs;
*   a register of use cases: document the specific tasks or processes Al supports (in particular to identify critical dependencies for increasingly BAU processes); and
*   risk assessment: identify where advanced models might intersect with personal data, sensitive data or critical decision-making processes and confirm key supply chains.

This approach clarifies potential areas of exposure in a fast-changing regulatory environment.

Once the current state of AI implementation in the organisation has been established, a risk assessment or gap analysis can be carried out to identify risk areas and facilitate the creation of a road map to AI compliance.

Any such road map will need to be dynamic, with periodic AI impact assessments being conducted to evaluate how AI is changing specific workflows and functions, such as client services. These risk management tools will help in adapting strategies and ensuring that the adoption of AI technologies yields the desired outcomes.

#### Establishment of internal documentation, policies and principles

Policies are vital to AI governance within an organisation. AI-specific procedures and policies are likely to be necessary, including, for example:

*   procurement guidelines: require thorough due diligence for third-party LLM service providers to ensure data handling and security practices meet legislative and internal compliance and procurement standards; and
*   acceptable use of generative Al: outline the permissible contexts for using LLMs internally, emphasising constraints related to training data or sensitive company information.

Policies should also either address topics such as data protection, privacy, non-discrimination and accountability or interweave with existing policies on those topics (which may require updating). For instance, an AI non-discrimination policy might require regular reviews of AI systems to ensure they do not perpetuate bias or inequality.

It may also be necessary to establish a dedicated AI legal technology team to be responsible for monitoring regulatory and ethical compliance to ensure the company can remain informed about regulatory changes and ethical considerations surrounding AI.

Processes also need to be updated to maintain compliance and transparency in AI usage. This may include establishing procedures for addressing consumer complaints and enquiries about AI, conducting an annual AI inventory review to evaluate the systems’ alignment with operational and ethical standards, and monitoring adherence to the AI framework for early issue detection and escalation, as well as regular board engagement on AI.

Existing compliance teams covering these areas are likely to need to collaborate to holistically monitor and address new legislative developments, particularly those governing high-risk AI systems.

Companies will also need to consider establishing a comprehensive AI audit trail, encompassing AI system specifications, data handling procedures, training protocols and performance records. These records are essential for auditing AI systems, understanding their decision-making pathways and outcomes (insofar as currently possible), and providing transparency to clients and regulators.

Finally, regular review of AI testing feedback, incident responses and regulatory developments are also likely to be prudent to ensure the organisation’s AI systems operate within evolving legal frameworks and ethical boundaries.

#### Security controls

Global organisations will also need to establish a secure environment that protects against unauthorised access, data breaches and potential misuse, incorporating physical, technical and administrative measures.

Many such measures should fall within the scope of an organisation’s existing cybersecurity framework and controls, to the extent that AI is deployed locally. Appropriate care, and contractual protections, will need to be taken when a company is relying on AI solutions provided by a third party as a service, to address and minimise the risk of exposure of any company data transferred to third parties.

It is likely that there will also be certain AI-specific cybersecurity risks that are not addressed by a company’s current cybersecurity controls; for example, the ability of adversaries to extract training data from large language models or novel risks such as prompt injection. Companies will accordingly need to take particular care where any AI product is public-facing (as compared with in-house processes that are not externally exposed), given the increased cybersecurity exposure and reputational risks to which a public-facing AI product may give rise.

#### Educate users of AI in an organisation

Incorporating AI within an organisation necessitates a robust compliance framework, including the education and training of the organisation’s employees. Educating users on the capabilities and limitations of AI, and the ethical considerations of its application will help to ensure effective and responsible use of the technology. In particular, employees will need to be alive to the tendency of current generative AI models to hallucinate responses, and the attendant need to critically assess any output for such issues.

Moreover, AI education programmes should cover the importance of data quality and the potential biases that can arise from inadequate data sets, as well as how to spot these issues in practice; for example, an AI system used for employment purposes and trained on historical data might inadvertently perpetuate past discriminatory hiring practices without appropriate safeguards.

By equipping employees with knowledge about how to use AI appropriately, how to ask the right questions and, in particular, how to assess AI outputs critically, organisations can start to mitigate known AI risks and foster an environment of compliance and ethical AI use.

Conclusion
----------

The integration of AI into business operations presents new compliance challenges shaped by divergent regulatory landscapes across jurisdictions, reflecting both mounting concerns around frontier LLMs, AI safety and consumer protection and also various governments’ desires to benefit from AI innovation and growth.

AI’s profound implications for regulatory compliance and risk management necessitate a proactive, dynamic and organisation-wide approach to risk management and compliance. A proactive AI compliance strategy can help to mitigate AI-associated risks, regulatory sanctions and reputational exposure.

As outlined above, such a strategy needs to be comprehensive, covering governance, employee education, policies, security measures and regular reviews encompassing not only the company’s compliance but also regulatory and technological developments.

The integration of AI into business operations is not merely a trend but a transformative movement with profound implications for regulatory compliance and risk management. By embedding compliance at each stage of AI deployment, and by proactively addressing the unique challenges posed by advanced generative Al models, organisations can position themselves to benefit from Al’s potential while mitigating the risks that accompany this fast-evolving technology.

Introduction Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has the potential to improve the delivery of government services and operations. GenAI enables enhancements to the development, adoption, and implementation of new technologies to streamline and optimize business operations and state services that California provides to its citizens. With that, it is critical for entities to be cognizant to ensure that GenAI does not lead to a state in which human life, health, property, or the environment is endangered, nor have public services be solely contingent upon these systems. GenAI systems are to be used only to augment and improve workflows, not to replace or impair the services received by the public. As described in the State of California Report: Benefits and Risks of GenAI report, GenAI offers a wide variety of potential applications with varying impacts. Any application of GenAI tools within the California state government will adhere to appropriate protocols and testing procedures. To proactively address potential threats to state-owned information assets, privacy, and the welfare of California's citizens, the Statewide Information Management Manual (SIMM) 5305-F, GenAI Risk Assessment introduces a risk assessment methodology that will aid state entities in evaluating the risks associated with GenAI systems. This SIMM is to ensure alignment with: • Executive Order (EO) N-12-23, The White House Blueprint for a GenAI Bill of Rights • NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework Please note that a completed SIMM 5310-C Privacy Threshold Assessment and Privacy Impact Assessment must be accessible upon request. # 3 AI Risk Management Frameworks for 2025 + Best Practices

+2
